t: When Disaster Strikes, Medicaid Work Rules Add Barriers for Potential Enrollees

p: PO‘IPŪ, Hawai‘i — A month after Hurricane Lowell hit the island of Kauaʻi, downed trees, construction crews, and damaged homes dotted the neighborhoods. At the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort, where over 100 workers were laid off, heaps of sand blanketed the grounds, and the drained pool’s concrete deck crumbled into the beach, just steps away from the ocean.
On Kauaʻi, unemployment claims jumped from 69 before the September hurricane to
nearly two weeks afterward, with widespread layoffs in the tourism industry amid a

In times of emergencies, Medicaid provides a critical safety net for people to maintain healthcare coverage. But new work rules in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Donald Trump signed last year, have put Medicaid enrollees living in disaster-struck counties at risk of losing health insurance. The law requires many nondisabled adults enrolled in Medicaid in 43 states and Washington, D.C., to work, volunteer, or attend school at least 80 hours a month, with eligibility checks starting in January.
In most states, residents impacted by a disaster can be granted a short-term exemption from Medicaid work requirements. Eligibility largely relies

Those who live in counties affected by natural disasters may not need to comply with the work rules — one of several carve-outs intended to provide limited, short-term exceptions. However, it’s unclear whether those who lost jobs after Hurricane Lowell would be eligible for that exemption so many months later. The Trump administration hasn’t offered clear guidance on how long a state can apply the natural disaster exemption to enrollees.

Rochelle Ganotisi, a mother of five, and her boyfriend were laid off by Sheraton and are getting by with unemployment payments and part-time work. The union that represents the hotel’s hospitality workers secured them three months of health insurance. If Ganotisi isn’t hired back to her housekeeping job by then, she plans to apply for Medicaid, the federal-state program that provides health coverage to people with low incomes or disabilities.

p: Hawaiʻi Gov. Josh Green, a Democrat and practicing physician, emphasized the importance of quickly issuing disaster declarations, especially as changes to Medicaid are set to take effect. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services allowed states to

“It would be devastating if suddenly 40,000 or 50,000 people didn’t have their Medicaid benefits,” he said. “It could affect our rural hospitals, our nurse practitioners, our doctors, so timeliness is key.”
Hawaiʻi officials said they will keep people who don’t meet the work requirements enrolled until July.
At least 34 states, plus Washington, D.C.,

the optional hardship exemptions to those work requirements. So far, four states — Indiana, Iowa, Missouri, and Ohio — do not plan to adopt the exemptions, according to KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. All four were issued disaster declarations for severe storms and flooding this summer.

CMS spokesperson Timothy Foster told KFF Health News in a statement that states can request a longer duration for a hardship exemption if they can prove that barriers to demonstrating work requirements persist in disaster areas.

Tom Cotter, CEO of Health Response Alliance, a nonprofit focused on improving healthcare access in disasters, said that when people lose coverage they end up using emergency rooms and charitable clinics, among the few places that will treat patients regardless of their ability to pay.

“All of these are really stretched thin during an emergency because their patient load goes way up,” he said. “That makes it even more expensive for the healthcare system that is being otherwise also burdened for the disaster.”

With additional work requirements, “it is going to slow the economic recovery of any particular community,” Cotter said. “It’s going to require people to be thinking about how they’re paying for healthcare when they have a lot of other things to worry about.”

p: Six Nebraskans impacted by the disasters lost coverage because they did not comply with work requirements. In October, the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services reported it was reprocessing their eligibility now that they qualify for a hardship exemption.
Sarah Maresh, director of the Health Care Access program at the nonprofit advocacy group Nebraska Appleseed, said the early rollout of the Medicaid work requirements has been marred by uncertainty.

“This is part of the confusion that comes with the Medicaid work requirements, because it applies differently depending on your situation,” she said. “I think it’ll be very challenging for new applicants.”

After CMS published rules governing the exceptions to the work requirements, several Democratic states sued the agency. Their lawsuit cited the narrow time frame for securing natural disaster exceptions. The complaint argued that the lack of guidance burdens state Medicaid agencies determining eligibility.
In its
, CMS wrote that the restrictions ensure the exemption applies only when a disaster affects Medicaid enrollees’ ability to comply with work requirements.

p: In Trump’s second term, he has denied nearly a quarter of disaster and emergency declaration requests as of mid-November, a denial rate higher than that of any other presidential administration in more than two decades, KFF Health News found. While decision wait times have increased across the country, they’re more acute in states with Democratic governors. Those states experienced both significantly higher denial rates and longer decision times than states with Republican governors, according to 2026 analyses from
and

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied any politicization in Trump’s decisions on disaster relief. She wrote that his response to requests from states ensures appropriate use of taxpayer money and that federal funds are used to “supplement — not substitute” states’ obligations to respond to disasters.

Some who lost their jobs and don’t qualify for Medicaid have few resources to help them.

Oscar Cardova worked at The Terrace Hanalei, a restaurant on Kauaʻi’s North Shore that was significantly damaged in the hurricane. When the restaurant closed, he lost his employer-provided health insurance. Although he has a work permit visa from Peru, he was denied Medicaid because of his immigration status.
Cardova and his wife, Yesenia, live in their van. Yesenia has astigmatism and, without insurance, she will need to pay for glasses out-of-pocket, Cardova said. The cost is expected to be about $500.

The couple planned to work for two more years in the U.S. before returning to Peru. A month after the hurricane, they were still struggling to find work. In search of more job opportunities, they considered moving to Honolulu.
“Right now, we’re just surviving,” Cardova said. “We’re waiting to see what happens before making other decisions, because we can’t keep living like this.”
